name: Plecanatide
evidenceNote: Approved for two adult constipation conditions on the basis of four 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trials enrolling more than 3,000 people in total.
summary: Plecanatide (Trulance) is a once-daily peptide tablet that draws fluid into the gut, FDA-approved for adults with chronic constipation or IBS-C.
keyTakeaway: Plecanatide is a 16-amino-acid copy of uroguanylin, a natural gut peptide, taken as a daily tablet. It acts on the lining of the intestine, which pulls water into the bowel and speeds transit, and almost none of it reaches the blood. The FDA approved it as Trulance in 2017 for chronic idiopathic constipation and in 2018 for IBS-C (the constipation-predominant form of irritable bowel syndrome). In the trials, about 21% of people on the approved dose met a strict durable response target, against 10% to 13% on placebo. Diarrhea is the main side effect. It carries a boxed warning against use in children.

blocks.text: Plecanatide is a synthetic peptide of 16 amino acids held in shape by two internal disulfide bridges [1]. It is a structural analog of human uroguanylin, a natural gut peptide, and like uroguanylin it switches on a receptor called guanylate cyclase-C [1]. In the published phase 3 report it was described as the first uroguanylin analog approved for chronic idiopathic constipation [2]. It is sold as Trulance by Salix Pharmaceuticals [1].

Unlike most peptide drugs, plecanatide is swallowed as a tablet. It does not need to be absorbed to work, because its target sits on the inner surface of the intestine. After a standard dose, levels in the blood were too low to measure in most samples [1].

It treats two common, long-lasting bowel conditions. Chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC) means persistent hard or infrequent stools without an identifiable cause. Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) combines constipation with recurring abdominal pain [1].

Plecanatide and its active breakdown product bind to guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C), a receptor on the cells lining the intestine. Activating GC-C raises levels of cyclic GMP (cGMP), a signaling molecule, both inside and outside those cells [1].

Inside the cells, cGMP opens the CFTR channel, which releases chloride and bicarbonate into the gut. Water follows, softening stool and speeding its passage. Outside the cells, higher cGMP has been linked in animal models to lower activity of pain-sensing nerves in the gut, which may explain the pain relief seen in IBS-C [1].

Because the drug works from inside the gut, it does not need to reach the bloodstream, and the label reports negligible systemic availability after a standard dose [1]. Linaclotide, another approved constipation drug, acts on the same receptor and has its own entry in this library.

Yes. The FDA approved Trulance for adults with chronic idiopathic constipation on January 19, 2017, and added irritable bowel syndrome with constipation on January 24, 2018 [4]. It is a prescription medicine taken as a 3 mg tablet once a day, and the tablet can be crushed for people who have trouble swallowing [1].

blocks.text: Plecanatide is prescribed for adults with CIC or IBS-C [1]. Each condition was tested in two 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. The main outcome was strict: a responder had to show sustained improvement for most of the 12 weeks, not just a better average [1].

For CIC, a responder needed at least three complete spontaneous bowel movements in a week, plus at least one more than at baseline, for at least 9 of the 12 weeks and at least 3 of the last 4 [1]. In the published CIC trial, plecanatide 3 mg also raised the number of complete spontaneous bowel movements by about 2.5 a week, compared with 1.2 on placebo [2]. For IBS-C, a responder had to report both a 30% drop in worst abdominal pain and at least one extra complete bowel movement a week in the same week, for at least 6 of the 12 weeks [3].

These response rates mean most people in the trials did not meet the strict target on either plecanatide or placebo, and the gain from the drug was roughly 7 to 12 percentage points [1]. Improvement in bowel movement frequency was seen as early as the first week [1].

Diarrhea is the main side effect. In the CIC trials it affected 5% of people on plecanatide and 1% on placebo, and in the IBS-C trials 4.3% versus 1% [1]. Most cases began in the first four weeks. Severe diarrhea occurred in 0.6% to 1% of people taking the drug, sometimes within the first day [1]. About 2% of people in the CIC trials stopped because of diarrhea [1].

items: Boxed warning: plecanatide is not used in children under 6, because a single oral dose killed young mice through dehydration, and it is avoided in patients 6 to 17 years old; safety and effectiveness in anyone under 18 have not been established [1]
Not used in people with known or suspected mechanical bowel obstruction [1]
Less common effects included sinusitis, upper respiratory infection, bloating, gas, abdominal tenderness, and raised liver enzymes in a few patients [1]

blocks.text: If severe diarrhea occurs, the label says to suspend dosing and rehydrate the patient, since fluid loss is the main risk [1]. In the CIC trials, 4% of people on plecanatide stopped because of any side effect, compared with 2% on placebo [1].
